title: CALM Lab useRguide
text:
Welcome
This is the useRguide for the CALM Lab. It is intended to be a resource for new lab members to get up to speed with the tools and workflows that we use in the lab. It is also a reference for existing lab members to refresh their knowledge or learn new skills.

title: What is R?
text:
According to the R website

R is a free software environment for statistical computing and graphics.

Let’s unpack this.

Free is nice!
Statistical computing is a general term referring to a large class of techniques that involves statistics, machine learning, and more.
Graphics refers to creating visualizations of data and output from statistical computing.

It’s really all about data. We live in a world where data is everywhere. Our personal lives, the media, and our work are all filled with data. That data is hidden behind numbers stored in spreadsheets, databases, and other formats. A fundamental skill in the modern world is the ability to analyze and visualize data. R is a tool that can help you do just that.
R is a programming language. There are pros and cons to using a programming language over Excel and GUI (Graphical User Interface) applications with click-and-drag functionality. The pros are related to the fact that programming languages are more flexible, powerful, and reproducible than GUI applications. The cons are that programming languages have a steeper learning curve than GUI applications and there are often more than one way to do the same thing in a programming language (possibly leading to confusion).
Debates on which programming language you should learn and use are rampant on the internet and social media. Regardless of which programming language you learn, working with data through code provides a challenge that will open you up to the world of data. You will gain an appreciation for the level of mundanity and complexity that is involved in processing the vast amounts of data in this world. Through working with data yourself, you will also become a better consumer of data and information that you see in your own work, the news, and social media.
It all starts with gaining a basic level of proficiency in 1) working with data, 2) data visualization, and 3) statistical computation. The first few chapters of this guide will focus on these three areas. After that, you will be able to explore more advanced levels of data analysis and visualization.

title: Install and Setup
text:
Install Software
First things first, you need to install R and Positron and configure your environment in a way that is conducive to our workflow in the lab.
If you do not have R or Positron installed on your computer, then follow the install instructions below.
If you already have R or Positron installed on your computer, then you may want to update your installations.

title: Install and Setup
text:
Install R
Download and install R from the R Project website.

Go to the R Project website.
Click on the “CRAN” link under “Download, Packages” in the left-hand menu.
Choose the 0-Cloud mirror option.
Select the base installation (for Windows) or the Latest Release (for Mac) option.
Open and run the installer file that you downloaded. Follow the prompts to complete the installation.



Install Positron
Download and install Positron from the Positron website.

Go to the Positron website.
Click on the “Download” button.
Select the appropriate version for your operating system.
Open and run the installer file that you downloaded. Follow the prompts to complete the installation.

title: Install and Setup
text:
Update Software

Update R
Warning: When updating R (not RStudio), it may remove all packages you have installed.
First check what version of R you have installed by opening Positron and checking the R version number in the console when you start it up. If you have an R version older than 4.6.0, then you should update your R installation.
Use the installr package to update R on Windows. To do this, run the following code in the Positron console:
install.packages("installr")
library(installr)
updateR()


Update Positron
To update Positron, go to the Positron website and download the latest version for your operating system. Then, open and run the installer file that you downloaded. Follow the prompts to complete the installation.

title: Install and Setup
text:
Getting to Know Positron
While R is the programming language that we will be using, Positron is the software that we will use to write and run R code. Positron is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for R. It provides a user-friendly interface for writing and running R code, as well as tools for debugging and visualizing data.
Open Positron and go through the Welcome Tour and Setup Guides to get familiar with the interface and features.

title: Install and Setup
text:
Configure Positron
Have a lab member or Dr. Tsukahara walk you through the Positron interface, and help you configure the settings to match the lab’s workflow. The following sections provide a summary of the recommended settings.

Install Extensions
To install an extension, click the Extensions icon (left sidebar) and search for the extension name.
Feel free to explore the available extensions, but the following are recommended for our lab workflow:

Fira Code — a fancy monospaced font with ligatures (e.g., != becomes ≠).
Material Icon Theme — icon themes change the look of folders and files.
One Dark Pro — a dark theme for your IDE.
GitHub Theme — a light theme for your IDE.
vscode-pets — adds a cute pet to your IDE.



Opening Settings

Press Cmd, or click the gear icon (bottom-left) → Settings.
In the Settings window, click the Search settings bar at the top and type in the name of the setting you want to change. The list of settings will filter as you type.

Special cases
